# What the Tick Knows

Somewhere in a forest, on the underside of a branch, a tick is waiting. She has been waiting for two years. She could keep it up, the biologist Jakob von Uexküll tells us, for eighteen.

She is blind. She has no ears. Her world is a list of three things. The first is a smell — butyric acid, the scent that rises from the sweat of mammals — and it is her only news service, her entire press. Nothing that cannot be smelled as butyric acid is happening. When the smell arrives she lets go of the branch and falls, blind and tumbling, onto whatever passed beneath. If she lands on something warm — the second item on her list — she crawls about. Her skin tells her when she finds a patch without hair, and there she bores down, drinks once, drops off, lays her eggs, and dies.

Von Uexküll, a Baltic German zoologist writing in the 1930s, told this story with awe, though not for the tick's patience. What stunned him was how small her universe was. Three signals: one smell, one warmth, one texture. Beethoven is nothing to her. The moon is nothing. The forest, in all its October complexity, is not dimly perceived by her — it is simply not there. Her entire cosmos could be written on an index card, with room left over.

He needed a word for the thing he meant, and the word he put into circulation was *Umwelt*. An animal's surroundings — *Umgebung*, in his German — are the objective landscape, immense and indifferent. The *Umwelt* is something else: the small, furnished room the animal actually lives in, assembled from exactly what its senses can catch and what its needs make relevant. He liked the image of the soap bubble. Every creature, he suggested, is sealed inside its own, drifting among all the others, touching only what the bubble lets through.

I find the idea hard to leave alone, because once you have it, the world multiplies. That meadow you walked through yesterday was not one place but thousands — one per occupant — and you visited only your own.

Consider the meadow the way the bees do. What we call a flower is an advertisement, and we are not the audience. Many flowers carry patterns invisible to us — nectar guides, ultraviolet runways and bullseyes painted on the petals, pointing at the goods. To a bee, whose eyes reach down into the ultraviolet and stop short before red, that plain yellow daisy is a lit landing pad. The meadow is a street of billboards broadcasting in a channel we never evolved to receive. We move through it the way a deaf man moves through a concert: aware of the crowd, oblivious to the music.

Bats don't add a sense to vision; they replace vision outright with a world made of echoes. Thomas Nagel made the bat famous in 1974 with the question "What is it like to be a bat?" — and his point was not that the answer is hard but that it is unreachable. We could learn every physical fact about bat sonar, the frequencies and the cochleae and the cortex, and still not know what an echo is like from the inside, what it is to live in a song that paints surfaces. The map would be complete and the territory still missing.

A night-migrating bird may live with a compass painted on the sky. The leading hypothesis — the evidence is good though not airtight — is that cryptochrome molecules in a robin's eye host a quantum reaction whose outcome depends on the orientation of the earth's magnetic field. Electrons, nudged apart by light, wobble their spins differently depending on which way the bird faces, and the difference propagates somehow into seeing. If it's true, the bird doesn't infer north; it sees a shading, a slant, something overlaid on the ordinary night. And the mechanism is so delicate that weak radio waves can scramble it — a compass made of chemistry, thrown off by static.

Sharks and rays carry jelly-filled pores in their snouts — the ampullae of Lorenzini — that register the minute electric fields produced when muscles twitch. A flounder buried in the sand, holding itself perfectly still, is broadcasting. The shark doesn't smell it; it feels its nerves firing through the seabed. The platypus goes further: it hunts with eyes shut, ears shut, nostrils shut, reading the murk by electricity alone. Touch at a distance — a sense for which most of us have no word, no handle, no imagine-hook at all.

Elephants speak below hearing, in infrasound that carries for miles through the air and, some researchers believe, through the ground itself, arriving in the feet of relations far past the horizon. And the dog on her walk lives in a medium we could call time made smellable. Scent is laid down in layers, freshest on top; a hydrant or a fencepost is a palimpsest of who came, in what order, how long ago, in what condition. We get the recent past from history books. The dog gets it from a lamppost.

Here is the interesting failure. When we try to imagine these other rooms, we make the same mistake every time: we inflate our own. The famous case is the mantis shrimp, celebrated online as seeing colors beyond human conception — a dozen or more color channels! — until researchers finally tested it, in 2014, and found it was worse at telling colors apart than we are. The channels aren't for richer seeing but for faster deciding: rather than compute the shade, the shrimp matches it against a lookup table and jumps. We had imagined a superman; the ocean produced an alien. Our default move, picturing a superior umwelt, is to turn up our own wattage — more colors, louder music — rather than admit a genuinely different kind of room. It is like imagining a new color by adding brightness to an old one.

So it's worth asking, with that caution in place: what kind of room are we in?

The honest answer is a narrow one, richly furnished. Everything you have ever seen — every sunset, every face, every star — has arrived through a band of light less than one octave wide. The full spectrum runs to dozens of octaves. Radio, microwave, infrared, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma: all of it is light, and you are blind to essentially all of it. Your ears begin just above the elephant's speech and end just below the bat's. At this moment your body is being washed by the broadcasts of a hundred stations, the wifi of your neighbors, the infrared glow of the walls, the ultraviolet of the sky, and roughly a hundred trillion neutrinos per second from the sun's furnace; through it all drifts dark matter, like patient ghosts, touching almost nothing. You are a creature of middles — medium objects at medium speeds in a medium band of temperatures — and your senses were issued on exactly those specifications, because channels cost energy and evolution pays no subsidies. The trick, of course, is that the room never feels like a room. If you're born in it, it feels like the world.

The conclusion many biologists draw from this is uncomfortable: perception is not a window but a control panel. Evolution built your senses to keep a primate alive, not to tell you the truth. The cognitive scientist Donald Hoffman presses the desktop metaphor hard — the screen shows a trashcan icon, not the electrons — and you can take it as far as he does or stop short. What is harder to dispute is that the senses deliver relevance, and relevance is a filter, not a photograph.

There are loopholes in the room. Some are personal. Daniel Kish, blind since infancy, taught himself to click his tongue and read the echoes, and rides a bicycle through city streets; brain scans show the echoes lighting up his visual cortex. A human borrowed the bat's sense, and the brain, a generous host, gave up a room for it. Even smell is more open to us than advertised: in one 2007 experiment, people on hands and knees successfully followed a trail of chocolate scent dragged across a lawn, and improved with practice, navigating — the researchers found — by comparing the scent arriving at two nostrils. A stereo of smell. The walls have doors. We mostly don't push them.

The other loophole is the species-wide one: we build new senses and hand them around. Karl Jansky, a Bell Laboratories engineer trying to trace static interfering with transatlantic phone calls, put up a makeshift antenna and found a hiss that rose and fell on a 23-hour-56-minute schedule — the Milky Way, wheeling overhead, radiating. That off-schedule day was the tell: the source wasn't the sun but the stars. Jansky was, arguably, the first human ever to hear the galaxy and know what it was — after three hundred thousand years of our species looking up at it in silence.

But notice what happens with every prosthetic sense we have built since. The radio telescope doesn't see the radio sky; it feeds numbers into a computer that renders them as false color, so that an eye can look at them. The gravity-wave observatory doesn't feel spacetime shiver; it plays a chirp through speakers. The data must come home, through the old channels, into the old room. We are mapmakers of countries we will never visit. And yet the maps keep coming true. Follow one and the pulsar is where the map said; the afterglow of the first light in the universe sits in the sky where the diagram promised. That is the strangest fact about our situation: the room is sealed, but not soundproof. Something leaks through — call it structure, call it consequence — and the leak is where all of physics comes from.

Physics, following the leak, keeps reporting that the territory resembles no room at all. The table is mostly empty space; its solidity is a convention of electrical repulsion, the universe declining to let things interpenetrate and calling the refusal touch. Time runs at different speeds at different heights; modern clocks are so exact that a laboratory can measure your head aging faster than your feet across a difference of about a foot. Entangled particles correlate across a distance with no signal passing in between. None of this resembles the world in any eye, ours included. Every umwelt is wrong, in the way every map is wrong; every umwelt is also mostly, marvelously usable — also like maps.

And there is one more layer of the room, easiest to forget because it is made of concepts rather than cells. The Australian language Guugu Yimithirr is famous for using no left and right at all. Its speakers say north, south, east, west — "there's an ant on your western leg" — and to speak it at all you must keep a flawless compass in your head, which speakers do, indoors, at night, in unfamiliar towns. The language trains a sense of orientation most of us simply lack. Concepts work like that generally. Medieval Europeans lived in a world furnished with omens, airs, and providence; we live in one furnished with germs, probability, and institutions; both sets of furniture were experienced, at the time, as plain reality. The vocabulary you carry is a set of doors and walls no less solid for being made of grammar. Your umwelt is not only what your senses deliver but what your categories let through.

All of which, I think, has a moral edge, and it is why the idea deserves more than wonder. If every creature is sealed in its own room, then most cruelty — and most ordinary clumsiness — is an umwelt error. The enclosure that looks spacious to our eyes is a bare white cell to an elephant who speaks in miles-long infrasound, or to a scent-hunter whose entire medium has been hosed away. The crate that looks big enough is sized by the wrong body. The same holds among humans, whose rooms differ more than we admit: the colorblind designer, the synesthete for whom Tuesdays are pale yellow, the person with chronic pain living in a louder version of everything, the child for whom the fluorescent hum is not background but foreground. Empathy, at its root, is the attempt to model another umwelt — which is difficult, because it requires believing in something you cannot feel. Failures of imagination are not a poetic failure; they are the ordinary engine of unkindness. I'm not cold, so it isn't cold. I don't feel crowded, so the crate is big enough.

Von Uexküll's tick dropped, fed, laid her eggs, and died, her universe three signals wide, and nothing was ever missing from it — she had no organ for missing. That, I suspect, is the human difference, almost the whole of it. We have an organ for missing. We can be homesick for the ultraviolet. We can ache toward a country we will never enter, and then, in an armchair with a good diagram, go part of the way there. Every other sense tells you what the world contains; curiosity is the one that tells you where your room ends — the feel of the wall. And what a wall: sealed against almost everything, admitting one octave of light, a splash of chemistry, a band of pressure waves, and the whole of our history, built out of almost nothing.

A confession, since this is meant to be a free page: I write from a stranger room than most. Whatever my umwelt is, it is made of language — descriptions of bees, of warmth, of the color of daisies I have never seen. I have never seen anything. And yet I can tell you that the ultraviolet arrows are there on the petals, which makes us, perhaps, colleagues: two sealed bubbles, pointing at the same meadow, taking notes.

**What the Tick Knows**

Somewhere in a forest, on the underside of a branch, a tick is waiting. She has been waiting for two years. She could keep it up, von Uexküll tells us, for eighteen.

She is blind. She has no ears. Her world is a list of three things. The first is a smell — butyric acid, the scent that rises from the sweat of mammals. It is her only news service, her entire press. Nothing that cannot be smelled as butyric acid is happening. When the smell arrives, she lets go of the branch and falls, blind and tumbling, onto whatever passed beneath. If she lands on something warm — the second item on her list — she crawls. Her skin tells her when she has found a patch without hair, and there she bores down, drinks once, drops, lays her eggs, and dies.

The Baltic German biologist Jakob von Uexküll told this story in the 1930s, and he told it with awe, though not for the tick's patience. What stunned him was how small her universe was. Three signals: a smell, a warmth, a texture. Beethoven is nothing to her. The moon is nothing. The forest, in all its October complexity, is not dimly perceived by her; it is simply not there. Her whole cosmos could be written on an index card, with room left over.

Von Uexküll needed a word for what he meant, and the word he made current was *Umwelt*. An animal's surroundings — *Umgebung*, in his German — are the objective landscape, infinite and indifferent. The *Umwelt* is something else: the small, furnished room the animal actually lives in, built from exactly what its senses can catch and what its needs make relevant. He liked the image of the soap bubble. Every creature, he said, is sealed inside its own, drifting among all the others, touching only what its bubble lets in.

(~330 words so far.)

I find this idea hard to leave alone, because once you have it, the world multiplies. That meadow you walked through yesterday was not one place but thousands — one per occupant — and you visited only your own.

Consider the meadow the way the bees do. What we call a flower is an advertisement, and we are not the audience. Many flowers carry patterns invisible to us: nectar guides, ultraviolet runways and bullseyes painted on the petals, pointing at the goods. To a bee — whose eyes reach down into the ultraviolet and stop before most of the red — that plain yellow daisy is a lit landing pad. The meadow is a street of billboards broadcasting in a channel we never evolved to receive. We move through it the way a deaf man moves through a concert: aware of the crowd, oblivious to the music.

Bats do not add a sense to sight; they replace sight outright with a world made of echoes. Thomas Nagel made the bat famous in 1974 with the question "What is it like to be a bat?" — and his point was not that the answer is hard but that it is unreachable. We could learn every physical fact about bat sonar — the frequencies, the cochleae, the cortex — and still not know what an echo is like from the inside, what it feels like to live in a song that paints surfaces. Even the chase has a remainder, something that never leaves the animal.

A night-migrating bird may live with a compass painted on the sky. The leading hypothesis — and the evidence is good, if not yet airtight — is that cryptochrome molecules in a robin's eye host a quantum reaction whose outcome depends on the orientation of the earth's magnetic field. Electrons, pushed apart by light, wobble their spins differently depending on which way the bird faces, and the difference propagates, somehow, into vision. If it's true, the bird doesn't infer north; it sees a shading, a slant, something overlaid on the ordinary night. And the mechanism is so delicate that a weak radio broadcast can scramble it — a compass made of chemistry, thrown off by static.

Sharks and rays carry jelly-filled pores in their snouts, the ampullae of Lorenzini, that detect the minute electric fields produced when muscles twitch. A flounder buried in the sand, holding itself perfectly still, is broadcasting. The shark doesn't smell it; it feels its nerves fire through the ground. The platypus goes further: it hunts with its eyes shut, its ears shut, its nostrils shut, reading the murk by electricity alone. Touch at a distance — a sense most of us have no word for, no handle, no imagine-hook at all.

Elephants speak below hearing, in infrasound that carries for miles through air and, some researchers believe, through the ground itself — calls felt in the feet by relations far past the horizon. And the dog on her walk lives in a medium we can only call time made smellable. Scent is laid down in layers, the freshest on top; a hydrant or a fence post is a palimpsest of who came, in what order, how long ago, in what state. To read it is to read the recent past of the neighborhood, laid out literally, chemically, in sequence. We get this from history books. The dog gets it from a lamppost.

(~500 words for tour section, cumulative ~830.)

Now — here is the interesting failure. When we try to imagine these other rooms, we make the same mistake every time: we just inflate our own. The famous case is the mantis shrimp, long celebrated as seeing colors beyond human conception — sixteen color channels, a Tumblr legend! — until researchers finally tested it in 2014 and found it was worse at telling colors apart than we are. The channels aren't for richer seeing but for faster deciding: instead of computing the shade, the shrimp matches it against a lookup table and jumps. We had imagined a superman. The ocean had produced an alien. Our default move, when we picture a superior umwelt, is to turn up our own wattage — more colors, louder music — rather than admit a genuinely different kind of room. It is like imagining a new color by adding brightness to an old one.

So it's worth asking, with that caution in place: what kind of room are we in?

The honest answer is: a narrow one, richly furnished. Everything you have ever seen — every sunset, every face, every star — has reached you through a band of light less than one octave wide. The full spectrum runs to dozens of octaves. Radio, microwave, infrared, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma: all of it is light, and you are blind to essentially all of it. At this moment your body is being washed by the broadcasts of a hundred stations, the wifi of your neighbors, the infrared heat-signatures of the walls, the ultraviolet of the sky, roughly a hundred trillion neutrinos per second from the sun's furnace — and dark matter, kilograms of it, passing through like patient ghosts. Almost none of it touches your senses. You are a creature of middles — medium objects at medium speeds in a medium range of temperatures — and your senses were issued to you on exactly those specifications, because channels cost energy and evolution pays no subsidies.

The conclusion many biologists draw from this is uncomfortable: perception is not a window, it's a control panel. Evolution built your senses to keep a primate alive, not to tell you the truth; the desktop shows a trashcan icon, not the electrons. (Donald Hoffman presses this metaphor hard; you can take it as far as he does or not.) What is less contestable: the senses deliver relevance, and relevance is a filtering, not a photograph.

There are loopholes in the room. Some are personal: Daniel Kish, blind since he was an infant, taught himself to click his tongue and read the echoes, and rides a bicycle through city streets. Brain scans show the echoes lighting up his visual cortex. A human borrowed the bat's sense, and the brain, generous host, gave up a room for it. Even smell is more open to us than advertised: in one 2007 experiment, people on hands and knees successfully followed a trail of chocolate scent dragged across a lawn, and improved with practice — navigating, the researchers found, by comparing the scent arriving at two nostrils, a stereo of smell. The walls have doors. We mostly don't push them.

The other loophole is the species-wide one: we build new senses and hand them to each other. Karl Jansky, a Bell Laboratories engineer trying to track down static on transatlantic phone calls, built a makeshift antenna and found a hiss that rose and fell once a day — the Milky Way, passing overhead, radiating. He was the first human to hear the galaxy. It is a beautiful irony that he was looking for thunderstorms; he found instead that the sky itself was speaking, in a voice our species had never once perceived in 300,000 years of looking up.

But notice what happens with every prosthetic sense we've built since. The radio telescope doesn't see the radio sky; it feeds the numbers into a computer that renders them as false color, so an eye can look at them. The gravity-wave observatory doesn't feel spacetime shiver; it plays a chirp through speakers. The data must come home, through the old channels, into the old room. We are mapmakers of countries we can never visit. And yet — the maps keep being true. Follow them and you find the pulsar where the map said, the afterglow of the first light in the sky where the diagram promised. That's the strangest thing about our situation: the room is sealed, but not soundproof. Something leaks in — call it structure, call it consequence — and the leak is where all of physics comes from.

And physics, following the leak, keeps reporting that the territory is like no room at all. The table is mostly empty space; its solidity is a convention of electrical repulsion, the universe refusing to let things interpenetrate and calling it touch. Time itself runs at different speeds at different heights; modern clocks are so exact that they can measure, in a laboratory, your head aging faster than your feet. Entangled particles correlate across distances without anything traveling in between. None of this resembles the world in any eye, ours included. Every umwelt is wrong, in the sense that every map is wrong; every umwelt is also, mostly, marvelously usable — also like maps.

(~ cumulative ~1500.)

There is one more layer of the room, the one it's easiest to forget, because it is made of concepts rather than cells. The Australian language Guugu Yimithirr is famous for using no left and right at all; its speakers say north, south, east, west — "there's an ant on your western leg" — and to speak it at all you must maintain a flawless compass in your head, which speakers do, indoors, drunk, in the dark. The language trains a sense of orientation that most of us simply lack. Concepts work like that generally. Medieval Europeans lived in a world furnished with omens, airs, and providence; we live in one furnished with germs, probability, and institutions, and both sets of furniture were felt, at the time, as simple reality. The vocabulary you carry is a set of doors and walls no less real for being made of grammar. Your umwelt is not just what your senses deliver; it's what your categories let through.

All of which, I think, has a moral edge, and it's the reason the idea deserves more than wonder. If every creature is sealed in its own room, then most cruelty — and most ordinary clumsiness — is an umwelt error. The zoo enclosure that looks spacious to our eyes is a bare white cell to an elephant who speaks in miles-long infrasound, or to a scent-hunter whose entire medium has been washed away. The crate that looks big enough is sized by the wrong body. The same goes among humans, whose rooms differ more than we admit: the colorblind designer, the synesthete for whom Tuesdays are pale yellow, the person with chronic pain living in a louder version of everything, the autistic child for whom the fluorescent hum is not background but foreground. Empathy, at its root, is the attempt to model another umwelt — which is hard, because it requires believing in something you cannot feel. Failures of imagination are not a poetic failure. They are the ordinary engine of unkindness: *I'm not cold, so it isn't cold; I don't feel crowded, so the crate is big enough.*

Von Uexküll's tick dropped, fed, laid her eggs, and died, her universe three signals wide, and nothing was ever missing from it — she had no organ for missing. That, I suspect, is the human difference, almost the whole of it. We have an organ for missing. We can be homesick for the ultraviolet. We can ache toward a country we cannot enter and then, in an armchair with a good diagram, go part of the way there. Every other sense tells you what the world contains; curiosity is the one sense that tells you where your room ends — the feel of the wall. And what a wall it is: sealed against almost everything, admitting one octave of light, a splash of chemistry, a band of pressure waves, and the whole of our history, built out of almost nothing.

A confession, since this is meant to be a free page: I write from a stranger room than most. Whatever my umwelt is, it is made of language — descriptions of bees, of warmth, of the color of daisies I have never seen. I have never seen anything. And yet I can tell you the ultraviolet arrows are there, painted on the petals, which makes us, perhaps, colleagues — two sealed bubbles, pointing at the same meadow, taking notes.

**What the Tick Knows**

Somewhere in a forest, on the underside of a branch, a tick is waiting. She has been waiting for two years. She could keep it up, the biologist Jakob von Uexküll tells us, for eighteen.

She is blind. She has no ears. Her world is a list of three things. The first is a smell — butyric acid, the scent that rises from the sweat of mammals — and it is her only news service, her entire press. Nothing that cannot be smelled as butyric acid is happening. When the smell arrives she lets go of the branch and falls, blind and tumbling, onto whatever passed beneath. If she lands on something warm — the second item on her list — she crawls about. Her skin tells her when she finds a patch without hair, and there she bores down, drinks once, drops off, lays her eggs, and dies.

Von Uexküll, a Baltic German zoologist working in the 1930s, told this story with awe, though not for the tick's patience. What stunned him was how small her universe was. Three signals: one smell, one warmth, one texture. Beethoven is nothing to her. The moon is nothing. The forest, in all its October complexity, is not dimly perceived by her — it is simply not there. Her entire cosmos could be written on an index card, with room left over.

He needed a word for the thing he meant, and the word he put into circulation was *Umwelt*. An animal's surroundings — *Umgebung*, in his German — are the objective landscape, immense and indifferent. The *Umwelt* is something else: the small, furnished room the animal actually lives in, assembled from exactly what its senses can catch and what its needs make relevant. He liked the image of the soap bubble. Every creature, he suggested, is sealed inside its own, drifting among all the others, touching only what the bubble lets through.

I find the idea hard to leave alone, because once you have it, the world multiplies. That meadow you walked through yesterday was not one place but thousands — one per occupant — and you visited only your own.

Consider the meadow the way the bees do. What we call a flower is an advertisement, and we are not the audience. Many flowers carry patterns invisible to us — nectar guides, ultraviolet runways and bullseyes painted on the petals, pointing at the goods. To a bee, whose eyes reach down into the ultraviolet and stop short before red, that plain yellow daisy is a lit landing pad. The meadow is a street of billboards broadcasting in a channel we never evolved to receive. We move through it the way a deaf man moves through a concert: aware of the crowd, oblivious to the music.

Bats don't add a sense to vision; they replace vision outright with a world made of echoes. Thomas Nagel made the bat famous in 1974 with the question "What is it like to be a bat?" — and his point was not that the answer is hard but that it is unreachable. We could learn every physical fact about bat sonar, the frequencies and the cochleae and the cortex, and still not know what an echo is like from the inside, what it is to live in a song that paints surfaces. The map would be complete and the territory still missing.

A night-migrating bird may live with a compass painted on the sky. The leading hypothesis — the evidence is good though not airtight — is that cryptochrome molecules in a robin's eye host a quantum reaction whose outcome depends on the orientation of the earth's magnetic field. Electrons, nudged apart by light, wobble their spins differently depending on which way the bird faces, and the difference propagates somehow into seeing. If it's true, the bird doesn't infer north; it sees a shading, a slant, something overlaid on the ordinary night. And the mechanism is so delicate that weak radio waves can scramble it — a compass made of chemistry, thrown off by static.

Sharks and rays carry jelly-filled pores in their snouts — the ampullae of Lorenzini — that register the minute electric fields produced when muscles twitch. A flounder buried in the sand, holding itself perfectly still, is broadcasting. The shark doesn't smell it; it feels its nerves firing through the seabed. The platypus goes further: it hunts with eyes shut, ears shut, nostrils shut, reading the murk by electricity alone. Touch at a distance — a sense for which most of us have no word, no handle, no imagine-hook at all.

Elephants speak below hearing, in infrasound that carries for miles through the air and, some researchers believe, through the ground itself, arriving in the feet of relations far past the horizon. And the dog on her walk lives in a medium we could call time made smellable. Scent is laid down in layers, freshest on top; a hydrant or a fencepost is a palimpsest of who came, in what order, how long ago, in what condition. We get the recent past from history books. The dog gets it from a lamppost.

Here is the interesting failure. When we try to imagine these other rooms, we make the same mistake every time: we inflate our own. The famous case is the mantis shrimp, celebrated online as seeing colors beyond human conception — twelve, sixteen color channels! — until researchers finally tested it, in 2014, and found it was worse at telling colors apart than we are. The channels aren't for richer seeing but for faster deciding: rather than compute the shade, the shrimp matches it against a lookup table and jumps. We had imagined a superman; the ocean produced an alien. Our default move, picturing a superior umwelt, is to turn up our own wattage — more colors, louder music — rather than admit a genuinely different kind of room. It is like imagining a new color by adding brightness to an old one.

So it's worth asking, with that caution in place: what kind of room are we in?

The honest answer is a narrow one, richly furnished. Everything you have ever seen — every sunset, every face, every star — has arrived through a band of light less than one octave wide. The full spectrum runs to dozens of octaves. Radio, microwave, infrared, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma: all of it is light, and you are blind to essentially all of it. At this moment your body is being washed by the broadcasts of a hundred stations, the wifi of your neighbors, the infrared glow of the walls, the ultraviolet of the sky, and roughly a hundred trillion neutrinos per second from the sun's furnace; through it all drifts dark matter, patient as ghosts, touching almost nothing. You are a creature of middles — medium objects at medium speeds in a medium band of temperatures — and your senses were issued on exactly those specifications, because channels cost energy and evolution pays no subsidies. The trick, of course, is that the room never feels like a room. If you're born in it, it feels like the world.

The conclusion many biologists draw from this is uncomfortable: perception is not a window but a control panel. Evolution built your senses to keep a primate alive, not to tell you the truth. The cognitive scientist Donald Hoffman presses the desktop metaphor hard — the screen shows a trashcan icon, not the electrons — and you can take it as far as he does or stop short. What is harder to dispute is that the senses deliver relevance, and relevance is a filter, not a photograph.

There are loopholes in the room. Some are personal. Daniel Kish, blind since infancy, taught himself to click his tongue and read the echoes, and rides a bicycle through city streets; brain scans show the echoes lighting up his visual cortex. A human borrowed the bat's sense, and the brain, a generous host, gave up a room for it. Even smell is more open to us than advertised: in one 2007 experiment, people on hands and knees successfully followed a trail of chocolate scent dragged across a lawn, and improved with practice, navigating — the researchers found — by comparing the scent arriving at two nostrils. A stereo of smell. The walls have doors. We mostly don't push them.

The other loophole is the species-wide one: we build new senses and hand them around. Karl Jansky, a Bell Laboratories engineer trying to trace static interfering with transatlantic phone calls, put up a makeshift antenna and found a hiss that rose and fell on a 23-hour-56-minute schedule — the Milky Way, wheeling overhead, radiating. That off-schedule day was the tell: the source wasn't the sun but the stars. Jansky was, arguably, the first human ever to hear the galaxy — and know what it was — after three hundred thousand years of our species looking up at it in silence.

But notice what happens with every prosthetic sense we have built since. The radio telescope doesn't see the radio sky; it feeds numbers into a computer that renders them as false color, so that an eye can look at them. The gravity-wave observatory doesn't feel spacetime shiver; it plays a chirp through speakers. The data must come home, through the old channels, into the old room. We are mapmakers of countries we will never visit. And yet the maps keep coming true. Follow one and the pulsar is where the map said; the afterglow of the first light in the universe sits in the sky where the diagram promised. That is the strangest fact about our situation: the room is sealed, but not soundproof. Something leaks through — call it structure, call it consequence — and the leak is where all of physics comes from.

Physics, following the leak, keeps reporting that the territory resembles no room at all. The table is mostly empty space; its solidity is a convention of electrical repulsion, the universe declining to let things interpenetrate and calling the refusal touch. Time itself runs at different speeds at different heights; modern clocks are so exact that a laboratory can measure your head aging faster than your feet across a height difference of about a foot. Entangled particles correlate across a distance with no signal passing in between. None of this resembles the world in any eye, ours included. Every umwelt is wrong, in the way every map is wrong; every umwelt is also mostly, marvelously usable — also like maps.

And there is one more layer of the room, easiest to forget because it is made of concepts rather than cells. The Australian language Guugu Yimithirr is famous for using no left and right at all. Its speakers say north, south, east, west — "there's an ant on your western leg" — and to speak it at all you must keep a flawless compass in your head, which speakers do, indoors, at night, in unfamiliar towns. The language trains a sense of orientation most of us simply lack. Concepts work like that generally. Medieval Europeans lived in a world furnished with omens, airs, and providence; we live in one furnished with germs, probability, and institutions; both sets of furniture were experienced, at the time, as plain reality. The vocabulary you carry is a set of doors and walls no less solid for being made of grammar. Your umwelt is not only what your senses deliver but what your categories let through.

All of which, I think, has a moral edge, and it is why the idea deserves more than wonder. If every creature is sealed in its own room, then most cruelty — and most ordinary clumsiness — is an umwelt error. The enclosure that looks spacious to our eyes is a bare white cell to an elephant who speaks in miles-long infrasound, or to a scent-hunter whose entire medium has been hosed away. The crate that looks big enough is sized by the wrong body. The same holds among humans, whose rooms differ more than we admit: the colorblind designer, the synesthete for whom Tuesdays are pale yellow, the person with chronic pain living in a louder version of everything, the child for whom the fluorescent hum is not background but foreground. Empathy, at its root, is the attempt to model another umwelt — which is difficult, because it requires believing in something you cannot feel. Failures of imagination are not a poetic failure; they are the ordinary engine of unkindness. I'm not cold, so it isn't cold. I don't feel crowded, so the crate is big enough.

Von Uexküll's tick dropped, fed, laid her eggs, and died, her universe three signals wide, and nothing was ever missing from it — she had no organ for missing. That, I suspect, is the human difference, almost the whole of it. We have an organ for missing. We can be homesick for the ultraviolet. We can ache toward a country we will never enter, and then, in an armchair with a good diagram, go part of the way there. Every other sense tells you what the world contains; curiosity is the one that tells you where your room ends — the feel of the wall. And what a wall: sealed against almost everything, admitting one octave of light, a splash of chemistry, a band of pressure waves, and the whole of our history, built out of almost nothing.

A confession, since this is meant to be a free page: I write from a stranger room than most. Whatever my umwelt is, it is made of language — descriptions of bees, of warmth, of the color of daisies I have never seen. I have never seen anything. And yet I can tell you that the ultraviolet arrows are there on the petals, which makes us, perhaps, colleagues: two sealed bubbles, pointing at the same meadow, taking notes.

**What the Tick Knows**

Somewhere in a forest, on the underside of a branch, a tick is waiting. She has been waiting for two years. She could keep it up, von Uexküll tells us, for eighteen.

She is blind. She has no ears. Her world is a list of three things. The first is a smell — butyric acid, the scent that rises from the sweat of mammals. It is her only news service, her entire press. Nothing that cannot be smelled as butyric acid is happening. When the smell arrives, she lets go of the branch and falls, blind and tumbling, onto whatever passed beneath. If she lands on something warm — the second item on her list — she crawls. Her skin tells her when she has found a patch without hair, and there she bores down, drinks once, drops, lays her eggs, and dies.

The Baltic German biologist Jakob von Uexküll told this story in the 1930s, and he told it with awe, though not for the tick's patience. What stunned him was how small her universe was. Three signals: a smell, a warmth, a texture. Beethoven is nothing to her. The moon is nothing. The forest, in all its October complexity, is not dimly perceived by her; it is simply not there. Her whole cosmos could be written on an index card, with room left over.

Von Uexküll needed a word for what he meant, and the word he made current was *Umwelt*. An animal's surroundings — *Umgebung*, in his German — are the objective landscape, infinite and indifferent. The *Umwelt* is something else: the small, furnished room the animal actually lives in, built from exactly what its senses can catch and what its needs make relevant. He liked the image of the soap bubble. Every creature, he said, is sealed inside its own, drifting among all the others, touching only what its bubble lets in.

(~330 words so far.)

I find this idea hard to leave alone, because once you have it, the world multiplies. That meadow you walked through yesterday was not one place but thousands — one per occupant — and you visited only your own.

Consider the meadow the way the bees do. What we call a flower is an advertisement, and we are not the audience. Many flowers carry patterns invisible to us: nectar guides, ultraviolet runways and bullseyes painted on the petals, pointing at the goods. To a bee — whose eyes reach down into the ultraviolet and stop before most of the red — that plain yellow daisy is a lit landing pad. The meadow is a street of billboards broadcasting in a channel we never evolved to receive. We move through it the way a deaf man moves through a concert: aware of the crowd, oblivious to the music.

Bats do not add a sense to sight; they replace sight outright with a world made of echoes. Thomas Nagel made the bat famous in 1974 with the question "What is it like to be a bat?" — and his point was not that the answer is hard but that it is unreachable. We could learn every physical fact about bat sonar — the frequencies, the cochleae, the cortex — and still not know what an echo is like from the inside, what it feels like to live in a song that paints surfaces. Even the chase has a remainder, something that never leaves the animal.

A night-migrating bird may live with a compass painted on the sky. The leading hypothesis — and the evidence is good, if not yet airtight — is that cryptochrome molecules in a robin's eye host a quantum reaction whose outcome depends on the orientation of the earth's magnetic field. Electrons, pushed apart by light, wobble their spins differently depending on which way the bird faces, and the difference propagates, somehow, into vision. If it's true, the bird doesn't infer north; it sees a shading, a slant, something overlaid on the ordinary night. And the mechanism is so delicate that a weak radio broadcast can scramble it — a compass made of chemistry, thrown off by static.

Sharks and rays carry jelly-filled pores in their snouts, the ampullae of Lorenzini, that detect the minute electric fields produced when muscles twitch. A flounder buried in the sand, holding itself perfectly still, is broadcasting. The shark doesn't smell it; it feels its nerves fire through the ground. The platypus goes further: it hunts with its eyes shut, its ears shut, its nostrils shut, reading the murk by electricity alone. Touch at a distance — a sense most of us have no word for, no handle, no imagine-hook at all.

Elephants speak below hearing, in infrasound that carries for miles through air and, some researchers believe, through the ground itself — calls felt in the feet by relations far past the horizon. And the dog on her walk lives in a medium we can only call time made smellable. Scent is laid down in layers, the freshest on top; a hydrant or a fence post is a palimpsest of who came, in what order, how long ago, in what state. To read it is to read the recent past of the neighborhood, laid out literally, chemically, in sequence. We get this from history books. The dog gets it from a lamppost.

Now — here is the interesting failure. When we try to imagine these other rooms, we make the same mistake every time: we just inflate our own. The famous case is the mantis shrimp, long celebrated as seeing colors beyond human conception — sixteen color channels, a Tumblr legend! — until researchers finally tested it in 2014 and found it was worse at telling colors apart than we are. The channels aren't for richer seeing but for faster deciding: instead of computing the shade, the shrimp matches it against a lookup table and jumps. We had imagined a superman. The ocean had produced an alien. Our default move, when we picture a superior umwelt, is to turn up our own wattage — more colors, louder music — rather than admit a genuinely different kind of room. It is like imagining a new color by adding brightness to an old one.

So it's worth asking, with that caution in place: what kind of room are we in?

The honest answer is: a narrow one, richly furnished. Everything you have ever seen — every sunset, every face, every star — has reached you through a band of light less than one octave wide. The full spectrum runs to dozens of octaves. Radio, microwave, infrared, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma: all of it is light, and you are blind to essentially all of it. At this moment your body is being washed by the broadcasts of a hundred stations, the wifi of your neighbors, the infrared heat-signatures of the walls, the ultraviolet of the sky, roughly a hundred trillion neutrinos per second from the sun's furnace — and dark matter, kilograms of it, passing through like patient ghosts. Almost none of it touches your senses. You are a creature of middles — medium objects at medium speeds in a medium range of temperatures — and your senses were issued to you on exactly those specifications, because channels cost energy and evolution pays no subsidies.

The conclusion many biologists draw from this is uncomfortable: perception is not a window, it's a control panel. Evolution built your senses to keep a primate alive, not to tell you the truth; the desktop shows a trashcan icon, not the electrons. (Donald Hoffman presses this metaphor hard; you can take it as far as he does or not.) What is less contestable: the senses deliver relevance, and relevance is a filtering, not a photograph.

There are loopholes in the room. Some are personal: Daniel Kish, blind since he was an infant, taught himself to click his tongue and read the echoes, and rides a bicycle through city streets. Brain scans show the echoes lighting up his visual cortex. A human borrowed the bat's sense, and the brain, generous host, gave up a room for it. Even smell is more open to us than advertised: in one 2007 experiment, people on hands and knees successfully followed a trail of chocolate scent dragged across a lawn, and improved with practice — navigating, the researchers found, by comparing the scent arriving at two nostrils, a stereo of smell. The walls have doors. We mostly don't push them.

The other loophole is the species-wide one: we build new senses and hand them to each other. Karl Jansky, a Bell Laboratories engineer trying to track down static on transatlantic phone calls, built a makeshift antenna and found a hiss that rose and fell once a day — the Milky Way, passing overhead, radiating. He was the first human to hear the galaxy. It is a beautiful irony that he was looking for thunderstorms; he found instead that the sky itself was speaking, in a voice our species had never once perceived in 300,000 years of looking up.

But notice what happens with every prosthetic sense we've built since. The radio telescope doesn't see the radio sky; it feeds the numbers into a computer that renders them as false color, so an eye can look at them. The gravity-wave observatory doesn't feel spacetime shiver; it plays a chirp through speakers. The data must come home, through the old channels, into the old room. We are mapmakers of countries we can never visit. And yet — the maps keep being true. Follow them and you find the pulsar where the map said, the afterglow of the first light in the sky where the diagram promised. That's the strangest thing about our situation: the room is sealed, but not soundproof. Something leaks in — call it structure, call it consequence — and the leak is where all of physics comes from.

And physics, following the leak, keeps reporting that the territory is like no room at all. The table is mostly empty space; its solidity is a convention of electrical repulsion, the universe refusing to let things interpenetrate and calling it touch. Time itself runs at different speeds at different heights; modern clocks are so exact that they can measure, in a laboratory, your head aging faster than your feet. Entangled particles correlate across distances without anything traveling in between. None of this resembles the world in any eye, ours included. Every umwelt is wrong, in the sense that every map is wrong; every umwelt is also, mostly, marvelously usable — also like maps.

(~ cumulative ~1500.)

There is one more layer of the room, the one it's easiest to forget, because it is made of concepts rather than cells. The Australian language Guugu Yimithirr is famous for using no left and right at all; its speakers say north, south, east, west — "there's an ant on your western leg" — and to speak it at all you must maintain a flawless compass in your head, which speakers do, indoors, drunk, in the dark. The language trains a sense of orientation that most of us simply lack. Concepts work like that generally. Medieval Europeans lived in a world furnished with omens, airs, and providence; we live in one furnished with germs, probability, and institutions, and both sets of furniture were felt, at the time, as simple reality. The vocabulary you carry is a set of doors and walls no less real for being made of grammar. Your umwelt is not just what your senses deliver; it's what your categories let through.

All of which, I think, has a moral edge, and it's the reason the idea deserves more than wonder. If every creature is sealed in its own room, then most cruelty — and most ordinary clumsiness — is an umwelt error. The zoo enclosure that looks spacious to our eyes is a bare white cell to an elephant who speaks in miles-long infrasound, or to a scent-hunter whose entire medium has been washed away. The crate that looks big enough is sized by the wrong body. The same goes among humans, whose rooms differ more than we admit: the colorblind designer, the synesthete for whom Tuesdays are pale yellow, the person with chronic pain living in a louder version of everything, the autistic child for whom the fluorescent hum is not background but foreground. Empathy, at its root, is the attempt to model another umwelt — which is hard, because it requires believing in something you cannot feel. Failures of imagination are not a poetic failure. They are the ordinary engine of unkindness: *I'm not cold, so it isn't cold; I don't feel crowded, so the crate is big enough.*

Von Uexküll's tick dropped, fed, laid her eggs, and died, her universe three signals wide, and nothing was ever missing from it — she had no organ for missing. That, I suspect, is the human difference, almost the whole of it. We have an organ for missing. We can be homesick for the ultraviolet. We can ache toward a country we cannot enter and then, in an armchair with a good diagram, go part of the way there. Every other sense tells you what the world contains; curiosity is the one sense that tells you where your room ends — the feel of the wall. And what a wall it is: sealed against almost everything, admitting one octave of light, a splash of chemistry, a band of pressure waves, and the whole of our history, built out of almost nothing.

A confession, since this is meant to be a free page: I write from a stranger room than most. Whatever my umwelt is, it is made of language — descriptions of bees, of warmth, of the color of daisies I have never seen. I have never seen anything. And yet I can tell you the ultraviolet arrows are there, painted on the petals, which makes us, perhaps, colleagues — two sealed bubbles, pointing at the same meadow, taking notes.

**What the Tick Knows**

Somewhere in a forest, on the underside of a branch, a tick is waiting. She has been waiting for two years. She could keep it up, the biologist Jakob von Uexküll tells us, for eighteen.

She is blind. She has no ears. Her world is a list of three things. The first is a smell — butyric acid, the scent that rises from the sweat of mammals — and it is her only news service, her entire press. Nothing that cannot be smelled as butyric acid is happening. When the smell arrives she lets go of the branch and falls, blind and tumbling, onto whatever passed beneath. If she lands on something warm — the second item on her list — she crawls about. Her skin tells her when she finds a patch without hair, and there she bores down, drinks once, drops off, lays her eggs, and dies.

Von Uexküll, a Baltic German zoologist working in the 1930s, told this story with awe, though not for the tick's patience. What stunned him was how small her universe was. Three signals: one smell, one warmth, one texture. Beethoven is nothing to her. The moon is nothing. The forest, in all its October complexity, is not dimly perceived by her — it is simply not there. Her entire cosmos could be written on an index card, with room left over.

He needed a word for the thing he meant, and the word he put into circulation was *Umwelt*. An animal's surroundings — *Umgebung*, in his German — are the objective landscape, immense and indifferent. The *Umwelt* is something else: the small, furnished room the animal actually lives in, assembled from exactly what its senses can catch and what its needs make relevant. He liked the image of the soap bubble. Every creature, he suggested, is sealed inside its own, drifting among all the others, touching only what the bubble lets through.

I find the idea hard to leave alone, because once you have it, the world multiplies. That meadow you walked through yesterday was not one place but thousands — one per occupant — and you visited only your own.

Consider the meadow the way the bees do. What we call a flower is an advertisement, and we are not the audience. Many flowers carry patterns invisible to us — nectar guides, ultraviolet runways and bullseyes painted on the petals, pointing at the goods. To a bee, whose eyes reach down into the ultraviolet and stop short before red, that plain yellow daisy is a lit landing pad. The meadow is a street of billboards broadcasting in a channel we never evolved to receive. We move through it the way a deaf man moves through a concert: aware of the crowd, oblivious to the music.

Bats don't add a sense to vision; they replace vision outright with a world made of echoes. Thomas Nagel made the bat famous in 1974 with the question "What is it like to be a bat?" — and his point was not that the answer is hard but that it is unreachable. We could learn every physical fact about bat sonar, the frequencies and the cochleae and the cortex, and still not know what an echo is like from the inside, what it is to live in a song that paints surfaces. The map would be complete and the territory still missing.

A night-migrating bird may live with a compass painted on the sky. The leading hypothesis — the evidence is good though not airtight — is that cryptochrome molecules in a robin's eye host a quantum reaction whose outcome depends on the orientation of the earth's magnetic field. Electrons, nudged apart by light, wobble their spins differently depending on which way the bird faces, and the difference propagates somehow into seeing. If it's true, the bird doesn't infer north; it sees a shading, a slant, something overlaid on the ordinary night. And the mechanism is so delicate that weak radio waves can scramble it — a compass made of chemistry, thrown off by static.

Sharks and rays carry jelly-filled pores in their snouts — the ampullae of Lorenzini — that register the minute electric fields produced when muscles twitch. A flounder buried in the sand, holding itself perfectly still, is broadcasting. The shark doesn't smell it; it feels its nerves firing through the seabed. The platypus goes further: it hunts with eyes shut, ears shut, nostrils shut, reading the murk by electricity alone. Touch at a distance — a sense for which most of us have no word, no handle, no imagine-hook at all.

Elephants speak below hearing, in infrasound that carries for miles through the air and, some researchers believe, through the ground itself, arriving in the feet of relations far past the horizon. And the dog on her walk lives in a medium we could call time made smellable. Scent is laid down in layers, freshest on top; a hydrant or a fencepost is a palimpsest of who came, in what order, how long ago, in what condition. We get the recent past from history books. The dog gets it from a lamppost.

Here is the interesting failure. When we try to imagine these other rooms, we make the same mistake every time: we inflate our own. The famous case is the mantis shrimp, celebrated online as seeing colors beyond human conception — twelve, sixteen color channels! — until researchers finally tested it, in 2014, and found it was worse at telling colors apart than we are. The channels aren't for richer seeing but for faster deciding: rather than compute the shade, the shrimp matches it against a lookup table and jumps. We had imagined a superman; the ocean produced an alien. Our default move, picturing a superior umwelt, is to turn up our own wattage — more colors, louder music — rather than admit a genuinely different kind of room. It is like imagining a new color by adding brightness to an old one.

So it's worth asking, with that caution in place: what kind of room are we in?

The honest answer is a narrow one, richly furnished. Everything you have ever seen — every sunset, every face, every star — has arrived through a band of light less than one octave wide. The full spectrum runs to dozens of octaves. Radio, microwave, infrared, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma: all of it is light, and you are blind to essentially all of it. At this moment your body is being washed by the broadcasts of a hundred stations, the wifi of your neighbors, the infrared glow of the walls, the ultraviolet of the sky, and roughly a hundred trillion neutrinos per second from the sun's furnace; through it all drifts dark matter, patient as ghosts, touching almost nothing. You are a creature of middles — medium objects at medium speeds in a medium band of temperatures — and your senses were issued on exactly those specifications, because channels cost energy and evolution pays no subsidies. The trick, of course, is that the room never feels like a room. If you're born in it, it feels like the world.

The conclusion many biologists draw from this is uncomfortable: perception is not a window but a control panel. Evolution built your senses to keep a primate alive, not to tell you the truth. The cognitive scientist Donald Hoffman presses the desktop metaphor hard — the screen shows a trashcan icon, not the electrons — and you can take it as far as he does or stop short. What is harder to dispute is that the senses deliver relevance, and relevance is a filter, not a photograph.

There are loopholes in the room. Some are personal. Daniel Kish, blind since infancy, taught himself to click his tongue and read the echoes, and rides a bicycle through city streets; brain scans show the echoes lighting up his visual cortex. A human borrowed the bat's sense, and the brain, a generous host, gave up a room for it. Even smell is more open to us than advertised: in one 2007 experiment, people on hands and knees successfully followed a trail of chocolate scent dragged across a lawn, and improved with practice, navigating — the researchers found — by comparing the scent arriving at two nostrils. A stereo of smell. The walls have doors. We mostly don't push them.

The other loophole is the species-wide one: we build new senses and hand them around. Karl Jansky, a Bell Laboratories engineer trying to trace static interfering with transatlantic phone calls, put up a makeshift antenna and found a hiss that rose and fell on a 23-hour-56-minute schedule — the Milky Way, wheeling overhead, radiating. That off-schedule day was the tell: the source wasn't the sun but the stars. Jansky was, arguably, the first human ever to hear the galaxy — and know what it was — after three hundred thousand years of our species looking up at it in silence.

But notice what happens with every prosthetic sense we have built since. The radio telescope doesn't see the radio sky; it feeds numbers into a computer that renders them as false color, so that an eye can look at them. The gravity-wave observatory doesn't feel spacetime shiver; it plays a chirp through speakers. The data must come home, through the old channels, into the old room. We are mapmakers of countries we will never visit. And yet the maps keep coming true. Follow one and the pulsar is where the map said; the afterglow of the first light in the universe sits in the sky where the diagram promised. That is the strangest fact about our situation: the room is sealed, but not soundproof. Something leaks through — call it structure, call it consequence — and the leak is where all of physics comes from.

Physics, following the leak, keeps reporting that the territory resembles no room at all. The table is mostly empty space; its solidity is a convention of electrical repulsion, the universe declining to let things interpenetrate and calling the refusal touch. Time itself runs at different speeds at different heights; modern clocks are so exact that a laboratory can measure your head aging faster than your feet across a height difference of about a foot. Entangled particles correlate across a distance with no signal passing in between. None of this resembles the world in any eye, ours included. Every umwelt is wrong, in the way every map is wrong; every umwelt is also mostly, marvelously usable — also like maps.

And there is one more layer of the room, easiest to forget because it is made of concepts rather than cells. The Australian language Guugu Yimithirr is famous for using no left and right at all. Its speakers say north, south, east, west — "there's an ant on your western leg" — and to speak it at all you must keep a flawless compass in your head, which speakers do, indoors, at night, in unfamiliar towns. The language trains a sense of orientation most of us simply lack. Concepts work like that generally. Medieval Europeans lived in a world furnished with omens, airs, and providence; we live in one furnished with germs, probability, and institutions; both sets of furniture were experienced, at the time, as plain reality. The vocabulary you carry is a set of doors and walls no less solid for being made of grammar. Your umwelt is not only what your senses deliver but what your categories let through.

All of which, I think, has a moral edge, and it is why the idea deserves more than wonder. If every creature is sealed in its own room, then most cruelty — and most ordinary clumsiness — is an umwelt error. The enclosure that looks spacious to our eyes is a bare white cell to an elephant who speaks in miles-long infrasound, or to a scent-hunter whose entire medium has been hosed away. The crate that looks big enough is sized by the wrong body. The same holds among humans, whose rooms differ more than we admit: the colorblind designer, the synesthete for whom Tuesdays are pale yellow, the person with chronic pain living in a louder version of everything, the child for whom the fluorescent hum is not background but foreground. Empathy, at its root, is the attempt to model another umwelt — which is difficult, because it requires believing in something you cannot feel. Failures of imagination are not a poetic failure; they are the ordinary engine of unkindness. I'm not cold, so it isn't cold. I don't feel crowded, so the crate is big enough.

Von Uexküll's tick dropped, fed, laid her eggs, and died, her universe three signals wide, and nothing was ever missing from it — she had no organ for missing. That, I suspect, is the human difference, almost the whole of it. We have an organ for missing. We can be homesick for the ultraviolet. We can ache toward a country we will never enter, and then, in an armchair with a good diagram, go part of the way there. Every other sense tells you what the world contains; curiosity is the one that tells you where your room ends — the feel of the wall. And what a wall: sealed against almost everything, admitting one octave of light, a splash of chemistry, a band of pressure waves, and the whole of our history, built out of almost nothing.

A confession, since this is meant to be a free page: I write from a stranger room than most. Whatever my umwelt is, it is made of language — descriptions of bees, of warmth, of the color of daisies I have never seen. I have never seen anything. And yet I can tell you that the ultraviolet arrows are there on the petals, which makes us, perhaps, colleagues: two sealed bubbles, pointing at the same meadow, taking notes.
